articles.title: The tech products we enthusiastically recommend this holiday season | TechCrunch
articles.summary: We've been reviewing a bunch of new gadgets at TechCrunch this year, and we have some clear favorites to share for your Black Friday shopping and beyond.
articles.body:
We’ve been reviewing a bunch of new gadgets and hardware at TechCrunch this year: dumb phones , bird feeders , health trackers , slushy machines , AI mattress pads , you name it. Sometimes we think they’re unnecessary and expensive , but other times, we try out devices that we love so much that we go out and buy them ourselves.

If these products can impress a group of (sometimes) curmudgeonly tech reporters, then they’re sure to please whoever you’re shopping for this holiday season.

We’ve reviewed a lot of e-readers this year. What can we say? We’re nerds. We work for a tech website. But after trying devices from the usual suspects as well as some wildcards, we have recommendations. Evidently, 2026 was the year we fell in love with the pocket-sized e-reader.

Xteink X3 ($55) – a budget pick for someone techy

It’s an e-reader so small that it can fit in your wallet, or even magnetize to the back of your phone. Do you dream of a world where instead of scrolling Instagram when you’re waiting in line for coffee, you actually opt to read books? There’s really something special about the X3, and it’s only $55 during Xteink’s Black Friday sale. Fair warning, it takes some fiddling with to set up, and it has no integration with Kindle, Libby, or any other apps, so only buy this for someone willing to do a bit of Reddit browsing and tinkering to get it up and running.

XTeink X4 Pro ($99) – it has a backlight!

If you aren’t planning to magnetize the XTeink to your phone, you’ve got to go with the X4 Pro . It’s slightly bigger, but it has a backlight, which makes it way more versatile. After using both the X3 and the X4 Pro, I find that the backlight really is a game changer, since I do a lot of reading in bed — plus, I like my Pop Socket wallet a bit too much to displace for the X3, and I’d rather just carry an extra credit card-sized device than risk forgetting my actual credit and ID cards, which I have grown too used to having on my phone.

Boox Palma Pro 2 ($400) – a phone-sized e-reader without the drawbacks

If I’m being honest, reading my colleague Aisha Malik’s review of the Boox Palma Pro 2 is making me want to buy one. I love using the Xteink e-readers, but they don’t connect to any outside apps. As a hardcore Libby power user (a phrase I am saying in earnest sincerity), it’s a bit frustrating that I can’t get my library books on Xteink e-readers. The same goes for apps like Kobo and Kindle, where any e-book you already own cannot be transferred out of the Amazon ecosystem unless the publisher agrees, which most do not.

If you’re looking for an e-reader with a screen that’s actually book-sized, my favorite that I’ve used is the Kobo Libra Colour , which is $259. The Amazon Paperwhite line is great, but c’mon, Amazon. Branch out!

Hey, we’ve all got to eat. And if you want, you can make that eating process overly techy. Why not?

Ember Mug 3 ($99) – for the tea lover who’s really particular

The Ember Mug 3 is the latest iteration in Ember’s line of coffee/tea cups that actually stay warm. Our reviewer Lauren Forristal especially appreciated that you no longer need to use your phone app to change the mug’s temperature, which seems like it would be really annoying!

This mug is perfect for gifting to someone, or to put on your own wishlist — you might not want to spend $99 on a mug for yourself, but these sorts of luxury, nice-to-haves are what holidays are made for!

Ninja Crispi Microwave and Air Fryer ($449.99) – two appliances in one!

Ah, Ninja, the premiere company in the business of turning every appliance into a two-in-one air fryer. I jest, but at least Ninja knows it’s onto something. Despite the high price point, Lauren says that this new product made “a pretty convincing case for ditching two appliances and making room for one.” You can’t buy more counter space (without moving), but you can buy more versatile appliances.

GoveeLife Smart Nugget Ice Maker Pro ($499.99) – if your fridge has a built-in ice maker, you just won’t understand

Sure, there are cheaper ice makers on the market. But Aisha clarifies that this is the ice maker for “those who crave what’s called ‘the good ice.’” If you feel so passionately about the ice in your beverages that you know what she means, then maybe this is for you.

What they really want is a Mac mini or Claude subscription, but if that’s out of budget, we have some other ideas that might impress your AI-pilled, vibe-coder loved ones…

Open AI Codex Micro ($230) – for the Codex evangelist

When I asked my colleague Lucas Ropek what about his favorite product he reviewed this year, he mentioned the Codex Micro . Some hard-core coders — who the product is aimed toward — have found this thing less than pleasing, but Lucas seems to have had fun figuring out this first attempt by OpenAI at hardware.

Best case, it’s a productivity game-changer for your friend who has a hardworking team of AI agents within the OpenAI ecosystem. Worst case, this will be a great piece of tech history in a few years.

For the person who’s desperate to log off

As people have become more conscious about how much time they spend online, new tech has emerged that, ironically, is designed to keep you away from tech. Some of these products can really make a difference in your life.

Brick ($59) or Brick Night ($129) — a not-so-subtle gift for your friend who doomscrolls every night before bed

For about six months, I’ve consistently used the Brick to prevent me from using social media as the last thing I do before bed, or the first thing in the morning. Some people use it to help them focus during the work day, but evidently, I was not the only one who needed Brick’s help with sleep. The company recently launched its second device, Brick Night, which “Bricks” your phone when you are in the same room. You can customize the times that the Brick Night is active, so it’s not as though you can never, ever use social media in your room. Both Brick and Brick Night are very customizable, so you can create the perfect set-up tailored to your needs.

It’s embarrassing how whole-heartedly I recommend the Brick, which is basically just a hunk of plastic with an NFC chip in it and a companion app. But my sleep has improved significantly — I even do 8 AM Pilates now. Who am I?

Dumb Phone ($20 + service plan) – for someone who wants to try something new but can’t totally give up their iPhone

I’ve tried out far pricier smart phone alternatives, but the Dumb Phone was both the most affordable, and the most usable for me. In the humble shell of a $20 TCL flip phone , Dumb Co loads its own software so that users can access apps like WhatsApp, Spotify, Apple Music, and Uber. You can even access iMessage through a third-party app, though Apple could probably get that shut down… no one tell Apple, please!

The Dumb Phone is particularly usable because it’s not intended to be a complete replacement for your smartphone — it’s more like a companion device that you can take out with you when you want to feel more present in the world but still may need to call an Uber home.

Wearable health trackers are pretty common nowadays, but after reviewing several different rings and wristbands , Aisha has named a winner.

There are a lot of ugly health trackers. And then there’s the Oura Ring 5 , the leading smart ring maker’s first product that’s thin enough to wear without loudly broadcasting to the world that you’re monitoring your heart rate. (For what it’s worth, I tried the RingConn 3 — which is about the same size as Oura Ring 5 — but returned it, unsatisfied. Womp womp.) Aisha notes in her review that the newest Oura ring is more durable, has a better battery life, and looks more premium than its predecessors.

articles.title: Apple’s first smart glasses are coming together
articles.summary: The company’s Siri AI-powered eyewear is set to be announced at WWDC next year.
articles.body: Apple’s smart glasses are among the worst-kept secrets in the tech world. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says the company’s first model, which will lack augmented reality features, will be announced at June’s WWDC next year. They likely won’t ship right away, however, with Gurman saying only that “glasses shipments would begin before the end of the year.” Key to their success will be the newly revamped Siri AI, which is adding fine-grained control over apps. By adding those features now and letting developers add support on the iPhone first, it’s hoping that its smart glasses will be able to hit the ground running. The prototypes, dubbed N50, are currently running a pared-down version of visionOS and a new processor based on its older smartwatch chips. They also have a MagSafe-like charger Gurman describes as “flat, rectangular” and “roughly the size of a Tic Tac,” which can be used even while still wearing the glasses. In addition to Apple putting an emphasis on style, privacy, and audio quality, the company is also hoping that Wi-Fi connectivity will grant them a certain amount of freedom, despite relying on an iPhone to actually execute many tasks: > The glasses have Wi-Fi, allowing certain functions outside of third-party apps to continue working when the iPhone isn’t nearby. Users could theoretically keep listening to audio over Wi-Fi after walking away from their phones, for instance, though the eyewear won’t operate as a fully independent device. Apple is also emphasizing the sound quality, which employees have said is industry-leading, with support for phone calls, music playback and FaceTime audio communication.

articles.summary: Estudantes de Rondônia premiadas no Manna Champion Chip recebem homenagem surpresa de piloto e emocionam famílias após vitória em evento de tecnologia.
articles.body:
Quatro estudantes de Pimenta Bueno (RO) foram surpreendidas por uma homenagem durante o voo de volta para Rondônia, após serem premiadas em um campeonato de tecnologia realizado em Campinas (SP). O piloto anunciou a conquista das alunas e pediu uma salva de palmas em reconhecimento à participação delas no evento.

“Queremos parabenizar hoje as alunas Aline, Rebeca, Tayla e Thamily, que participaram de um campeonato chamado Manna Champion Chip e foram premiadas, juntamente com a professora Michelle Sanches, com visitas aos laboratórios de microeletrônica na Unicamp. Parabéns a todas vocês e também à professora. Uma salva de palmas”, anunciou o piloto.

O momento foi registrado em vídeo e compartilhado nas redes sociais. As homenageadas são Thayla Lais Camillo Rodrigues, Thamily Almeida do Carmo, Rebeca Freisleben Teixeira e Aline Meloni Silva, estudantes da Escola Estadual Orlando Bueno da Silva.

🔎 As alunas participaram do Manna Chip Out 2026 , evento que reúne estudantes e educadores em atividades voltadas à tecnologia e à microeletrônica. A programação foi realizada nos dias 13 e 14 de novembro, em Campinas (SP), com acompanhamento das professoras Michelle Yamaguchi Sanches e Leide Daiane Nogueira Santos.

A equipe orientada pela professora Michelle conquistou o título de melhor equipe da Região Norte, resultado que garantiu a participação no evento. Durante a programação, as estudantes conheceram laboratórios e institutos de pesquisa da Universidade Estadual de Campinas (Unicamp) e participaram de atividades voltadas à tecnologia e à microeletrônica.

Para a professora Michelle, a experiência aproximou as estudantes do ambiente acadêmico e despertou o interesse delas pela área científica.

“Foi muito gratificante poder proporcionar esta experiência, com várias trocas de conhecimentos. Elas puderam conhecer diversos cientistas da área da microeletrônica. Observar que elas voltaram cheias de sonhos, querendo voltar para fazer a graduação na Unicamp, é maravilhoso”, destacou.

A professora Leide Daiane também acompanhou as estudantes na viagem. Ex-aluna da Escola Orlando Bueno, ela acredita que experiências como essa podem ampliar as perspectivas das meninas sobre o futuro.

“Me traz assim uma sensação de propósito participar desses momentos, sabe? Principalmente que muitas delas, só uma já tinha viajado de avião. Então, desde a viagem de avião até conhecer a Unicamp e viver toda essa experiência, eu sei que é algo de uma transformação social muito grande, vai ampliar o olhar delas para o mundo e para tudo que elas podem realizar na vida”, contou.

A homenagem durante o voo também emocionou os familiares das estudantes. Jesana Santos de Almeida, de 37 anos, mãe de Thamily, de 12, contou que ficou surpresa ao assistir ao vídeo compartilhado pela professora nos grupos de mensagens.

“Quando eu vi o vídeo sendo divulgado pela professora nos grupos, fiquei muito surpresa. Para mim, foi uma alegria muito grande. Eu me senti muito honrada e feliz por minha filha ter tido a oportunidade de a educação proporcionar essa experiência para ela”, relatou.

A mãe também destacou a felicidade da filha por representar a escola e o município em um evento de tecnologia.

“A minha filha ficou muito feliz, está muito feliz e honrada, sentindo-se privilegiada por ter tido essa oportunidade de representar também a escola onde estuda, Orlando Bueno, e a cidade de Pimenta Bueno, Rondônia. Para nós, foi um privilégio muito grande. Ela ainda está absorvendo tudo, porque foi muita coisa boa e muita experiência incrível”, afirmou.

Arlete Freisleben, de 44 anos, mãe de Rebeca Freisleben, de 15, também comemorou a conquista. Segundo ela, a filha sempre demonstrou interesse por desafios e se dedicou ao projeto desde o início.

"É indescritível a sensação de ver a filha se destacando. Realmente, não consigo encontrar uma palavra para definir exatamente o sentimento! Mas posso afirmar que é uma alegria que todas as famílias deveriam sentir pelo menos uma vez na vida!", afirmou Arlete.

Segundo Arlete, Rebeca voltou animada com as experiências e motivada pelos conselhos que recebeu durante a viagem. Uma das frases que mais a marcaram foi: "Se um pode, todos podem", como incentivo para continuar os estudos e buscar seus objetivos.

Já Creuziene Camillo, mãe de Thayla Lais, disse que a filha sempre se dedicou aos estudos e se preparou para viver oportunidades como essa. Ela também contou que ficou orgulhosa ao acompanhar a conquista.

"É uma experiência única. Ela foi atrás do sonho dela, para aprender mais, se aprofundar mais em coisas novas para o futuro. É o orgulho de toda mãe, ver o filho crescer na vida e eu como mãe, nossa, não tenho nem palavra para expressar a alegria que eu tenho, por Deus ter me presenteado com essa filha maravilhosa", disse.

A professora Michelle Yamaguchi participa do Programa de Residência em Microeletrônica Manna Champion Chip, que integra o ecossistema Manna Team. A iniciativa busca popularizar a microeletrônica por meio da formação de professores da educação básica, que repassam os conhecimentos aos estudantes da rede pública.

O programa é liderado pela professora e pesquisadora Linnyer Beatrys Ruiz Aylon, que atua na área de microeletrônica e incentiva a participação feminina nas ciências, especialmente nos campos da tecnologia e da microeletrônica.

articles.title: Amazon’s Zoox robotaxis are now available via Uber
articles.summary: Uber riders in Las Vegas can now hail Amazon’s Zoox robotaxis at no extra cost. Here’s how the MGM Resorts partnership works and when it’s coming to LA.
articles.body: Uber may be breaking up with Waymo, but it’s also gaining a new robotaxi BFF: Amazon. Starting today, Uber riders in Las Vegas can be matched with Amazon-owned Zoox’s purpose-built, bidirectional robotaxis. It’s a first for both companies: the first time Uber is adding a purpose-built, steering-wheel-free autonomous vehicle to its network, and the first time that Zoox is opening up its fleet to a third-party app. Uber says that anyone ordering an UberX, Uber Comfort, Uber Electric, Uber Comfort Electric, or Wait & Save in Sin City can get matched with a Zoox at no extra charge. Just like with Uber’s other AV partnerships (like Waymo in Phoenix and Austin, for now), riders can toggle a preference in the app’s Ride Preferences settings to boost their chances of getting an autonomous pod. Unlike Uber’s human drivers, Zoox has some geographic limitations. The company’s robotaxis only cover heavy tourist zones, like the Strip, downtown Las Vegas, and the Arts District. And Zoox isn’t abandoning its standalone app; it will continue to operate independently alongside the Uber integration. [Image: Image: Uber Alongside the launch, Uber and Zoox announced a multiyear deal making them the official rideshare and robotaxi partners for MGM Resorts International in Las Vegas. Anyone who has ever tried to catch a ride at the Bellagio or MGM Grand knows that resort pickup zones are notoriously chaotic. For autonomous vehicles, navigating sprawling, poorly mapped casino entrances — where valets, idling tour buses, and confused tourists all mill about — is a major technical headache. To keep Zoox’s pods from getting stuck in endless resort traffic loops, the partnership goes beyond simple branding. MGM, Uber, and Zoox say they are rolling out physical infrastructure tweaks, like clearer on-property wayfinding and custom in-app guidance designed to make pickups and drop-offs actually work smoothly for driverless cars. Uber and Zoox aren’t stopping at Vegas. The two companies already have their eyes their next major market: Los Angeles. Zoox plans to launch initial standalone operations in LA through its own app before the end of 2026, followed by a full Uber integration sometime in 2027. Uber’s playbook of welcoming a variety of small and large robotaxi players into its app came after the company pivoted away from building its own self-driving tech. Now it’s attempting to position itself as an indispensable platform for every autonomous vehicle operator, including Motional, WeRide, Avride, and Zoox. Of course, Uber’s strategy has had some drawbacks, too. Waymo co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana recently announced an end to her company’s exclusive partnership with Uber in Austin and Atlanta by January 2028, calling it a “crapshoot.”

articles.title: Willie Geist Will Exit MS NOW’s ‘Morning Joe’ After Nearly 20 Years for Expanded Role at NBC’s ‘Today’
articles.summary: MS NOW mainstay “Morning Joe” transformed suddenly into “Morning Whoa!” Monday when Willie Geist, the program’s longtime master of ceremonies, said he planne...
articles.body:
MS NOW mainstay "Morning Joe" transformed suddenly into "Morning Whoa!" Monday when Willie Geist, the program's longtime master of ceremonies, said he planned to leave his post at the end of the year for a broader role at NBC's "Today" franchise.

The maneuver will break up an A.M. team — Geist, Joe Scarborough and Mika Brzezinski– that has stayed together for about two decades, a rarity in the world of early-bird TV. "Morning Joe" launched on the cable network once known as MSNBC in April of 2007. Scarborough and Brzezinski remain under contract with MS NOW through 2029.

"Joe and Mika are truly family to me," says Geist, during a recent interview with Variety . Being part of the program, which is a must-watch for a certain swath of inside-the-Beltway denizens as well as political aficionados, "has given me everything in my career," Geist adds. "I was a producer at MSNBC when Joe had the idea that I should be on set with him and Mika, which made not a lot of sense." Nonetheless, it worked: "Morning Joe" has become essential viewing, particularly for an influential audience niche, and is one of the Versant-backed outlet's signature programs.

After the start of 2027, Geist will get time to spend not only on the "Sunday Today" telecast he has led for more than a decade , but also on a variety of extensions that include a longform podcast of the show's main interview, known as a "Sunday Sitdown." He will contribute stories to "Today" that may have him travel around the country for human-interest pieces, or unique interviews. And he will fill in for various anchors when their schedules call them away from "Today's" weekday hours.

Geist has, for the past year, enjoyed one of the most unique arrangements in the TV-news business.

He works during the week for "Morning Joe," where he often keeps a roundtable conversation flowing from New York while Scarborough and Brzezinski typically weigh in from Florida, and then works to craft a Sunday telecast of NBC News' "Today" that relies heavily on his writing sensibility and a deep-dive interview with a newsmaker or celebrity. He also fills in for various "Today" anchors like Craig Melvin and in the 10 a.m. hour as needed — a job that can pull him away from duties on "Morning Joe."

When MS NOW was part of the NBCUniversal media conglomerate, maintaining such a schedule — one in which he works in some capacity nearly every day of the week — was easier. Now that the cable-news outlet is part of a company, Versant, that was spun off from NBCU by corporate parent Comcast, the plan is more difficult to keep in motion.

"I think everyone agrees that this had to happen," Geist says.

Indeed, NBC News and MSNBC shared many personnel who contributed to both outlets, but only Geist was allowed to continue to do so following their split. Stephanie Ruhle and Steve Kornacki are among the journalists who had to pick sides , and NBC News in recent years has taken anchors who led hours on MSNBC, like Hallie Jackson and Craig Melvin, and gave them more duties at the broadcast operation.

"I was genuinely lucky to be able to do both," says Geist. "A lot of people didn't get that choice."

When MSNBC and NBC News were owned by the same company, studios for their programs were part of the company's complex at Rockefeller Plaza. Now that they've broken up, Geist finds himself hustling from Versant's headquarters through Times Square after "Morning Joe" ends to get over to NBC and tend to duties tied to "Today." There are times when he needs to be at "Today" during "Morning Joe," which can require him to leave one program early and rush over to join the other.

Geist's presence at "Morning Joe" has long been understated, but it is critical. He's the one who keeps the various contributors in New York teed up for commentary and reaction while Scarborough and Brzezinski offer viewpoints and perspective. Geist must be ready to spark conversation about a wide range of topics — and have some level of expertise in them all. "Part of the job I've loved at 'Morning Joe' is it's a freewheeling conversation," says Geist. "You have to be ready for everything. We are going to talk about the political stores of the day in great detail, not just gloss over them, but also the discussion might turn to music or movies or sports, or whatever it is. It's a real morning breakfast conversation."

In past interviews, Brzezinski and Scarborough have called their show partner essential. "The chemistry is Willie, Mika and me," Scarborough told Variety in 2020 , and when Geist takes off from the show on Mondays following his "Sunday Today" work, he said, "we really feel it."

MS NOW did not immediately name a successor for Geist.

The show has fared well in recent months. "Morning Joe" is the most-watched cable-news morning program among viewers in Washington, D.C., and has, year to date, seen its overall audience hike 24%, according to data from Nielsen, while viewership among people between 25 and 54, the demographic most coveted by advertisers in news programs, increase 57%. The audience for Fox News Channel's "Fox & Friends," however, is larger, as are the audiences for the three broadcast-network morning programs.

NBC News has spent more time working to monetize Geist's work on "Sunday Today." Once a quarter, he hosts one of his longform interviews in front of a paying audience in different parts of the country. NBC News in recent months has made a full video version of his "Sunday Sitdown" available on its digital platforms — a new way to reach audiences (and the advertisers who might follow them).

On TV, Geist says, the interview segments take up eight minutes, an eternity for the medium. Online, however, viewers may get 45 minutes to an hour of Geist quizzing subjects who over the years have included Mick Jagger, Paul McCartney or actor Ryan Reynolds.

"I like that, because nothing is lost," says Geist, who got his start in the business working for a CNN news venture with Sports Illustrated that hoped to vie with ESPN. "Everything we do is available to viewers and subscribers."

Geist will turn his focus to a Sunday program that has made some strides against its main competitor, CBS' "Sunday Morning." That program, a mainstay of the TV schedule, has seen its viewership decline this season, while the audience for Geist's show is on the rise.

Overall viewership for "Sunday Today" has risen 4% season to date as of November 8, according to data from Nielsen. Meanwhile, viewers between 25 and 54, the demographic coveted most by advertisers in news programming, are up 1%. The overall "Sunday Morning" audience is down 11% over the same period this season, while its demo viewership has fallen 9%.

"Sunday Morning" continues to draw a bigger crowd than "Sunday Today." An average of 4.41 million viewers watched the CBS program as of November 8, compared with 2.72 million for "Sunday Today."

Sundays for Geist may be something of a family line of business. His father, the legendary writer and columnist Bill Geist, was an integral part of "CBS Sunday Morning" for 31 years.

When the younger Geist first started anchoring NBC's Sunday morning program, his father was still working at CBS' stalwart during the time slot. "There were mornings when you could look up" at TV monitors tracking news programs "and I would be on one and my dad would be on the other," Geist recalls. He grew up being a part of a Sunday-morning news audience, which would pay attention "on a day when people were able to stop and take the time and look and listen and were not racing" to get to work or school. "I love that show and was inspired by it," he says.

Was he destined to pick up similar duties? "I don't know if it was fated, or if it just happened that way," Geist offers. No matter what brought him to the time period, Geist's presence there appears to be locked in for the foreseeable future.

articles.title: Audible is trying to make it easier to find audiobooks you’ll actually like
articles.summary: Audible is introducing an AI-assisted synopsis feature that helps users determine whether they’ll enjoy an audiobook before they start listening to it.
articles.body: Audible is introducing an AI-assisted synopsis feature that’s designed to help users determine whether they’ll enjoy an audiobook before they jump in and start listening to it. The new audio discovery feature combines audiobook samples, AI overviews, and author commentary to give users more information before choosing their next story, in addition to recommended audiobook collections that are personalized to individual listening tastes. Audio discovery provides a soundbite synopsis, with the aim of preventing Audible users from having to research titles on other platforms. The feature plays users a snippet of the audiobook and a brief AI-generated overview including its themes and listener reactions, drawing from reviews and other publicly available data. It can also include commentary from an author or Audible editor, which is pulled directly from past Audible interviews. “Picking your next listen should feel like getting a tip from a friend. With audio discovery, you’ll get a quick audio take on why the title might be right for you, from our editors, fellow listeners, or even the author,” Audible chief product and analytics officer Andy Tsao said in the announcement. “Some of the best listening experiences are those rare finds or hidden gems, and we want to make those great discoveries happen more often and more easily.” [Video: Audible audio discovery] Audio discovery is rolling out on select English-language titles in the US, with plans to eventually expand to other regions. Audible is also using AI to personalize audiobook collections around users’ listening tastes, in an effort to make titles that don’t appear on best-selling lists easier to discover. Like audio discovery, these personalized collections are rolling out to customers in the US, and also include commentary from Audible’s editors. [Image: Audible users in the US will also start seeing AI-curated recommendation categories based on what they usually listen to. These are the latest AI-powered features that Audible is introducing in an effort to attract new users and fend off growing competition from rival platforms like Spotify. As part of this update, Audible is also expanding two beta features: Ask a Question, which allows users to ask AI about characters, plot points, references, and more; and Recaps, which provides spoiler-free audio summaries of what the user has already listened to. These are now available for a “select set” of additional English-language titles in the US, according to Audible, with a broader rollout planned to start in December.

articles.title: US tightens AI chip export controls to deter Chinese companies from accessing compute remotely | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Under the interim rule, the U.S. will require firms to get licenses to export AI chips if they may provide compute to China or other restricted countries.
articles.body:
The Trump administration on Monday is preparing to roll out new export controls on AI chips and data centers outside the U.S., seeking to prevent companies, especially those in China, from getting past U.S. export controls by remotely accessing AI infrastructure located in other countries.

Under the interim rule , the Commerce Department will require companies to get licenses to export, reexport, or transfer AI chips and servers to data centers anywhere in the world if they may provide compute to companies in China or other restricted countries.

The remote-access rules target companies based in the U.S.’s D:5 group of embargoed countries, which includes China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, and 18 others.

The U.S. already has rules requiring chip companies to get a license to ship AI chips to companies based in, or owned by any business in, this group of countries.

“This new control is a logical extension of existing controls,” the interim rule reads. “These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models.”

The move comes days after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned amid a scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy linked to one of the chipmaker’s customers. The U.S. government has reportedly been wanting to put that customer, Megaspeed, on a special entity list, as it believes the company has been buying thousands of Nvidia chips to provide compute to Chinese businesses to get past existing export-control restrictions.

Reuters reported last week that Chinese AI companies are rushing to secure computing capacity overseas amid fears of tighter restrictions from the U.S.

The rule applies to data centers or any network that can supply over 12 million total processing performance (TPP), an export-control metric the U.S. uses to measure computing power. (Twelve million TPP roughly works out to the max computing power of about 750 Nvidia H100 or H200 chips.) The rule also covers indirect access through go-betweens or brokers, and exporters and data center operators are required to keep an eye on their customers’ ownership structures and activities to ensure they aren’t run by anyone from the D:5 group.

The rule also adds new licensing requirements for chip exports, reexports, or transfer of advanced semiconductors to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil. The Commerce Department said it had included these as they “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion.” For these countries, however, the license requirements will not apply to chips “destined” for companies based in the U.S.

Existing data center operators providing services that fall under this new rule are required to get licenses within 90 days of the rule coming into effect.

Notably, the rule doesn’t apply to commercial recommendation systems, like those used in e-commerce or social media.

The rule also rescinds the Biden admin’s AI Diffusion Rule from January 2025, which sought to impose country-level limits on exports of advanced AI chips, and restrict transfers of certain powerful AI models. That May, the Trump administration said it would throw out that framework, arguing that it added unnecessary restrictions on U.S. companies and the country’s allies.

“By making these changes, this IFR prevents the use of certain SI items in data centers and at a computing power level that can be used for training or running of advanced SI models,” the rule reads. “Access to such computing power can be used to train and run advanced SI models capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten U.S. national security or foreign policy interests.”

articles.title: 15 hotel guests were injured by chlorine poisoning due to Microsoft’s global email outage
articles.summary: Microsoft’s global Outlook email outage interrupted safety notifications about elevated chlorine levels in a German hotel’s pool, now its first post-mortem explains why it lasted so long.
articles.body: Microsoft’s worldwide 365 and Outlook outage had real-world consequences after it cut off email alerts for a German hotel’s pool safety system. The German outlet Westdeutscher Rundfunk (WDR) said several people were injured at a Phantasialand hotel on Friday after its email system failed to deliver a safety alert about elevated chlorine levels in the pool, as spotted earlier by NotebookCheck and TechRadar. A machine-translated Facebook post from a German fire department said it responded to a Phantasialand hotel after a “technical malfunction” caused an excessive amount of chlorine to enter a swimming pool, resulting in chlorine gas leaking into the surrounding area. As reported by WDR, 15 people were affected by the incident, including four who were transported to the hospital. Microsoft has since published a post-incident report about the outage, and EVP Charles Lamanna posted an abridged version last night on X. The company says three factors contributed significantly to the incident, including a bug introduced in a previous update in July. This, coupled with a surge in load following an earlier Teams outage and an “unrelated issue” from the previous day that knocked out nearly 14 percent of its server capacity, activated the conditions for the “latent” bug in the July update to rear its head, which “caused requests to build up until servers ultimately stopped responding” during the peak traffic window in the US on Thursday. The outage lasted from Thursday afternoon and well into Friday morning for many businesses on the East Coast, before Microsoft said service was fully restored on Sunday. “Recovery took longer than usual because as servers returned to service, they were immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic and became unresponsive again,” Microsoft says. “Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state.” Microsoft adds that it couldn’t “quickly revert the change” because the defect was a latent bug from several months ago.

articles.title: Apple adds ‘face unlock’ to the iPhone Duo, but it’s not Face ID
articles.summary: Apple's latest iOS 27.3 developer beta introduces a limited face unlock feature for the iPhone Duo, alongside other improvements.
articles.body:
One of the top complaints from tech reviewers about Apple’s new foldable, the iPhone Duo, has been its reliance on Touch ID, a technology that’s been largely replaced by Face ID across the company’s iPhone lineup.

With Monday’s release of iOS 27.3 beta for developers, Apple is addressing that complaint with a new “face unlock” feature that lets iPhone Duo users unlock their phones using the front camera, rather than waiting for a future hardware upgrade.

To be clear, this feature is not Face ID.

Due to hardware constraints, the iPhone Duo shipped without support for Face ID technology primarily because its thin, foldable design doesn’t offer enough space for the TrueDepth sensor array that Face ID requires. A recent report from Bloomberg suggests that the company is working to change that in a future version of the iPhone Duo. In the meantime, the Duo uses Touch ID for unlocking, authentication, and Apple Pay.

The new face unlock feature, however, will allow users to quickly unlock the device using the front camera when the phone is closed. It only works if users have recently authenticated with Touch ID or a passcode. Apple notes that Apple Pay and passwords will still require Touch ID, and users will have to authenticate with Touch ID again after 45 minutes of inactivity.

The move is meant to make it easier for people to use the Duo in the way they’re accustomed to, after years of unlocking an iPhone just by looking at it.

Apple isn’t going so far as to allow face unlock to work across the entire device, though, because the technology isn’t as secure as Face ID. The latter uses Apple’s TrueDepth 3D sensing hardware, which includes a flood illuminator and a dot projector that casts over 30,000 invisible infrared dots onto the user’s face to build a unique 3D map of the face. The system combines this map with attention-awareness checks, making it resistant to attempts to fool it with photos or other 2D images.

The software update addresses another complaint by incorporating one of the “hacks” iPhone Duo early adopters were using to force their phone to lock when they shut it. That involved creating a shortcut that would automatically run when the phone was closed. Now, Apple says users can enable this feature directly in Settings, under Display and Brightness.

Alongside the software update, Apple announced that more than 200,000 apps are now optimized for the iPhone Duo, up from over 100,000 earlier this month .

Other new features in this latest software release include an option to ask Siri questions about the content of a web page, even portions that aren’t visible without scrolling. Apple is also introducing video podcasts in Apple Podcasts in the Apple TV app, catching up with rivals like YouTube and Spotify.

Apple is also expanding access to Apple News puzzles for News+ subscribers in Australia, the U.K., and for French-Canadian users. Australian News+ subscribers will get access to a daily quick crossword, crossword mini, and Sudoku, as well as Apple’s original puzzles, Quartiles and Emoji Game . U.K. users will get the quick crossword, the crossword mini, and Sudoku, while French-Canadian subscribers will get access to Apple’s original puzzles.

The iOS 27.3 software update is currently available to developers and will soon arrive for public beta testers. It will roll out more broadly to all users after further testing is complete.

articles.title: Mercedes-Benz takes on Tesla FSD with new point-to-point city driving assist
articles.summary: Mercedes-Benz is launching MB.Drive Assist Pro and Hands-Free Highway Assist in the US in 2027, bringing Nvidia-powered point-to-point city navigation and 85 mph hands-free cruising to select vehicles.
articles.body: Mercedes-Benz is tossing its hat into the partial autonomy ring with the launch of two new features next year: hands-free highway driving and a point-to-point city navigation system. The new features will put the German automaker in competition with Tesla, which is currently leading the auto industry in the development of hands-free systems. Mercedes’ point-to-point driver assist feature, called MB.Drive Assist Pro, will handle most of the driving on local roads and in dense, urban traffic. Once a destination is plugged into the vehicle’s navigation, the system assists across the entire route, handling highway exits, lane changes, intersections, and traffic lights. But unlike Tesla’s Full Self-Driving, MB.Drive Assist Pro requires that drivers keep their hands on the wheel while navigating through cities. The system is powered by 27 sensors (10 cameras, 5 radars, 12 ultrasonic sensors) and a high-performance computer capable of 254 TOPS running on the new MB.OS architecture. That computer runs on Nvidia’s Drive AV stack, blending pure AI with a deterministic “Halos” safety guardrail layer. (We got to experience the point-to-point system as a passenger during a demonstration in San Francisco last year.) The Hands-Free Highway Assist, meanwhile, works similarly to GM’s Super Cruise or Ford’s BlueCruise, in that drivers are able to take their hands off the steering wheel when driving on approved, controlled-access highways. The highway assist can also handle speeds of up to 85 mph, which is a big jump from Mercedes’ previous generation Drive Pilot’s 40 mph limit. It also includes Proactive Lane Change Assist, which automatically initiates lane changes to pass slower cars or follow navigation toward an exit. Earlier this month, a number of journalists got to test out the new features in San Francisco. InsideEVs called it a “real challenger” to Tesla FSD, praising how confidently and predictably it handled double-parked trucks, construction zones, and pedestrians during a 25-minute downtown loop. The Drive noted that the system’s “confidence and fluidity” felt more assured than rival systems. And Verge contributor Tim Stevens (writing for Endgadget) said it handled jaywalkers, cyclists, and sudden U-turns “without issue” and took the stress out of city driving. Mercedes will begin rolling out both features via an invite-only access program in California next month, ahead of a broader nationwide launch in 2027 — with highway assist arriving in the spring. Eligible vehicles include the CLA Electric, GLC Electric, GLE, GLS, and S-Class, with more vehicles to follow in 2028. While Mercedes hasn’t announced exact pricing yet, eligible owners will be able to unlock the software over the air through the automaker’s online store using one-month, one-year, or three-year subscription plans. The launch of the new features comes after Mercedes paused development of a Level 3 system, in which drivers can take their eyes off the road, in addition to their hands off the wheel, during certain approved stretches of highway. By pivoting to hands-free highway driving and point-to-point city navigation, Mercedes is betting that its Nvidia-powered, Level 2 features will have more wide appeal — and less regulatory resistance.

articles.title: Attackers targeted iPhone users through some of the world's most-popular websites in attempt to steal: Full list of websites 'infected with malware'
articles.summary: A large-scale cyberattack exposed visitors to some of the world's most-visited websites to malware after attackers compromised the Optimizely Web
articles.body: A large-scale cyberattack exposed visitors to some of the world's most-visited websites to malware after attackers compromised the Optimizely Web experimentation platform, according to security researchers at Report URI. The campaign affected 178 organisations and used trusted website infrastructure to deliver malicious code to unsuspecting users. Researchers said the attackers injected malicious JavaScript into Optimizely customer projects, allowing malware to be served through websites that users would normally consider trustworthy. Because the malicious code was delivered through Optimizely's own content delivery network and security certificates, the attack was difficult to detect.What happenedReport URI researcher Scott Helme said the attackers wrote malicious code into customer projects on Optimizely Web, a platform many large companies use to run website experiments. Those sites load a script from Optimizely’s servers, so the malware arrived from a source they already trusted, without their own systems being breached. Helme said it is not known how the attacker gained access to so many unrelated accounts.iPhone and iPad users specifically targetedThe malware was designed to perform multiple malicious activities, including stealing cryptocurrency, capturing payment card details, collecting cookies and taking screenshots. For users visiting affected websites on Apple devices, the attackers also deployed the Coruna and DarkSword iOS exploit kits in an apparent attempt to compromise iPhones and iPads. Report URI said cryptocurrency had already been stolen during the campaign, with verified transactions traced to wallets controlled by the attackers.What the malware didThe script swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attacker’s, skimmed card details typed into sites’ own payment forms, and sent back cookies and page screenshots. On iPhones and iPads, it loaded two exploit kits, Coruna and DarkSword, that target older iOS versions. Report URI said iOS 18.7.3 and later, and iOS 26.3 and later, are patched. By 19:25 UTC on Monday, the attacker’s wallets had received about $7,040.Most malicious code now removedReport URI said remediation efforts appeared to be successful, with most of the malicious code removed by the time researchers completed their analysis. The number of infected snippets detected later in the day had fallen sharply compared with earlier findings. The incident highlights the growing risk posed by software supply-chain attacks, where hackers compromise third-party services used by multiple organisations, allowing them to reach large numbers of users without directly attacking each company individually.Clean-up and adviceMost of the malicious code was removed by Monday evening. At 21:52 UTC only TalkTalk’s script was still infected, Report URI said. articles.title: The Verge Best of 2026
articles.summary: The Verge’s top gadget picks for 2026, selected by members of the editorial staff.
articles.body: Hundreds of gadgets pass across our desks each year. Some leave their mark and get a full review or make it to the top of a buying guide. It’s harder than it sounds to narrow down our favorites. Instead of simply picking products that scored highly, or only those that made it into our buying guides, we asked our reviews team and staff at large to nominate their products of the year. Then our editors whittled the list down to the top 25, balancing categories like smart home, phones, laptops, and just cool stuff. The result is our Best of 2026 — a list of products our staff has purchased, reviewed, or just plain loves. It’s still mid-November, and we know new products are set to launch before the end of the year. So we may update this list if there’s anything we think deserves a spot before the ball drops on New Year’s Eve. Then we dive right into CES and start all over again in 2027. Without further ado… here are The Verge Best of 2026 winners. [Image: Roborock Saros 20 The Saros 20 is one of Roborock’s current flagship floor cleaners, but it distinguishes itself from the rest of the company’s robovacs with a pair of extending leglike appendages on the underside. It uses those legs to boost itself over obstacles, like uneven transitions between rooms. It’s highly maneuverable, thanks to its use of spinning mop pads instead of a heavy roller, and without a lidar tower protruding out the top. The Saros 20 is just 3.13 inches tall, small enough to squeeze under most furniture. It’s also equipped with excellent obstacle avoidance, and it uses a split brush design underneath with a gap, allowing hair and fibers to get quickly sucked instead of tangled up in bristles. — Andrew Liszewski, senior reporter [Image: Segway Navimow X430 The Navimow X430 came out on top of our robot lawnmower showdown earlier this year, and The Verge’s Jennifer Pattison Tuohy said it was “by far” the best one she tested. It was the only one that could mow her front and back yards in one trip, and the only one that didn’t get stuck. It even successfully rolled through potholes and over small tree branches. The Navimow X430’s 17-inch cutting width was also wider than the competition, helping it finish mowing faster. It navigates using a combination of technologies, but there’s also a handy remote control mode you can use to take over in sensitive spots in your yard, or to clean up stray grass fronds the bot missed. — Stevie Bonifield, news writer [Image: Fairphone 6 Plus The Fairphone 6 Plus is just a regular old Android phone, and that’s actually a triumph. Fairphone has been selling its repairable, ethically sourced phones for years now, and previous generations have been underpowered or come with serious compromises. The Fairphone 6 Plus doesn’t feel compromised in the same way, and it comes with swappable back panels with different accessories, like a wallet or grip. The $649 price feels entirely reasonable for what it offers, especially when you consider that you can take care of easy fixes, like swapping in a new battery yourself at minimal cost. In a year when we got a lot of bad RAMageddon-related news in the smartphone industry, the Fairphone 6 Plus felt like a relief. — Allison Johnson, senior reviewer [Image: iPhone 18 Pro The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max easily secured a spot on our Best of 2026 list. Apple didn’t change much in its winning formula this year but focused on what people care about most: camera and battery life. The biggest update is probably the main camera, which now has a variable aperture that lets photographers adjust background blur and take better low-light photos. The iPhone 18 Pro Max also has the longest battery life in an iPhone to date, while the iPhone 18 Pro lasts as long as last year’s 17 Pro Max. — Todd Haselton, deputy reviews editor [Image: Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Before there was the iPhone Duo, there was the Z Fold 8. Not by much — just a few months — but Samsung beat Apple to market with a passport-shaped foldable. It’s a little thinner, lighter, and narrower than the Duo, and that makes a real difference in how comfortable it is to use for long stretches of time. It’s not rated for the same level of dust resistance as the Duo, and it doesn’t feel quite as “premium,” but apps make better use of the cover screen. The more I hold it, the more I think Apple needs to take a page out of Samsung’s book here. — Allison Johnson, senior reviewer [Image: Bambu Lab P2S Combo 3D printing is finally something I can recommend to just about anyone with space for a 30-inch cube in their garage, because the Bambu Lab P2S Combo is the easiest printing experience I’ve touched. It prints beautifully out of the box but, more importantly, it keeps on printing with minimal care, maintenance, or fuss. I can leave rolls of colorful filament inside for months, then press a button on my phone to print, because the bundled AMS keeps them dry and automatically loads each one. Technically the P2S arrived in 2025, but I’d never buy a just-released 3D printer: I spent a year and over 1,700 hours of print time (and counting) to be sure of my recommendation. Wish Bambu treated the open-source community better, though. — Sean Hollister, senior editor [Image: Werewolf VFLEX When The Verge decided to do a Best of 2026, my mind immediately jumped to the nerdiest thing I’ve tested all year — a dongle that lets you power aging gadgets with the same USB-C cables that charge your laptop and phone. Lose your SNES power brick? Want to make a desktop monitor portable? Want to make a Game Boy run forever? Werewolf VFLEX can make those happen, and so much more. It’s like having a universal AC adapter, one you don’t even need to plug into the wall, because USB-C batteries are amazing. — Sean Hollister, senior editor [Image: Fitbit Air It’s no surprise that, given its provenance, the Fitbit Air is an excellent fitness tracker, even if its tracking capabilities don’t go as in depth as other devices. For $100, the Air comes with a thinner and more comfortable strap than Whoop’s bands, with a design that lets the sensor module be easily removed and swapped into other straps. Battery life is excellent, requiring just a handful of charges each month while the Air tracks metrics like steps, heart rate, sleep, blood oxygen, and cardio load. All of that data is available through the Google Health app without a subscription, but for $100 you can upgrade to Google Health Premium, which adds access to video workouts, adaptive fitness plans, and an AI health coach that can share summaries of your day or night and answer questions about your health. — Andrew Liszewski, senior reporter [Image: Liene Pearl N200 Pro photo printer I usually regret my TikTok shop purchases. Not this one. I was tired of filling my journals with muddy, blue-tinged photos from HP Sprocket that faded over time. The Liene Pearl N200 Pro uses dye sublimation, so the colors are super vivid. The app is easy to use, and it comes with 50 sheets and five ink cartridges. You can usually find it for $100 to $120, and refills cost just $25 for 50 sheets. That’s pretty affordable — especially if you love scrapbooking. — Victoria Song, senior reviewer [Image: Oura Ring 5 The Oura Ring 5 is thinner and lighter than the Oura Ring 4. The metal finish is more durable than Oura’s previous models, so nicks and scratches should be less of an issue. The case also adds support for on-the-go wireless charging, but unfortunately it’s sold separately. This year’s Oura Ring also dropped the smallest and largest size options. The Oura Ring 5 is still the best smart ring on the market, especially if you’re upgrading from an older model or are new to smart rings. — Stevie Bonifield, news writer [Image: Sony Bravia 9 II RGB LED TV 2026 is the year nearly every TV manufacturer released an RGB LED TV, which uses individual red, green, and blue LEDs to provide the backlight instead of a field of blue or white LEDs. The Sony Bravia 9 II is the best of the bunch, with accurate, vibrant color; the incredible processing that Sony is known for; and a really cool lenticular screen on the stand that hides the cables behind it. The first generation of a new technology is always a bit tricky, but Sony showed that an RGB LED TV can be done right. — John Higgins, TV & audio senior reviewer [Image: Sony XM4C headphones When Sony launched its WH-1000XM4C wireless headphones in October, there was a certain amount of smug satisfaction enjoyed by those of us who still prefer Sony’s six-year-old WH-1000XM4 headphones over its successors. Sony made significant design changes with the WH-1000XM5 and then walked a few of them back with the WH-1000XM6. Both have better active noise cancellation and battery life than Sony’s latest, but the new XM4C resurrects the XM4’s comfortable, compact folding design with a replaceable battery, so loyal fans of the original can enjoy the new version for years to come. — Andrew Liszewski, senior reporter [Image: Anker Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro The Liberty 5 Pro set a new bar for call quality this year. The Verge’s John Higgins said they delivered the best in-call noise canceling he’s ever heard, even compared with pricier headphones like Apple’s AirPods Pro 3. They run on Anker’s new Thus chip and feature 9.2mm drivers, active noise cancellation, and IP55 water resistance. The case also has a built-in display to quickly change settings like ANC or check the Liberty 5 Pro’s battery life, with separate icons for each earbud and the case itself. — Stevie Bonifield, news writer [Image: Apple Studio Display XDR There’s plenty about the Studio Display XDR to find interesting: It’s the first Apple 5K monitor with a mini-LED panel and quantum dots that has a peak brightness of 2,000 nits, it has an adaptive refresh rate up to 120Hz, and it has a bunch of color-accurate reference modes for a wide range of professional uses. But what got me most excited was the inclusion of Apple’s CMF 2026 color-matching function for its two general picture-mode presets. It’s a new display standard developed as an alternative to CIE 1931, the standard for the past 80 years, which can cause colors to look different across multiple narrow-band display technologies like OLED and mini-LED with quantum dots. Apple CMF 2026 aims to fix that, and I’m here for it. — John Higgins, TV & audio senior reviewer [Image: MacBook Neo The MacBook Neo, despite running on an iPhone chip, works pretty darn well as a MacBook, and that’s mostly all I need to say. Yes, it now starts at $699 instead of $599 because of RAMageddon, so it’s not as good of a deal as it was when it launched. But it’s a very functional laptop, still has a great keyboard and (mechanical!) trackpad, and comes in fun colors. Apple hit it out of the park with the Neo. — Jay Peters, senior reporter [Image: Framework 13 Pro Framework’s Laptop 13 Pro is my ideal all-purpose Windows laptop (or Linux, if you’re inclined). It’s portable, powerful, dabbles in 1080p gaming, and it’s even user-upgradable and repairable. It’s the Framework formula many of us have come to love, like those precious modular ports, but with a major step up in quality-of-life features: a haptic trackpad, a nice touchscreen, and a much-improved build. Its biggest fault is its price. That’s the toll RAMageddon has taken on everything this year — it just hit a smaller manufacturer like Framework harder. Yes, Framework chose an extra-pricey component in LPCAMM2 memory, but that’s also part of why the 13 Pro is so cool and forward-looking. — Antonio G. Di Benedetto, laptop reviewer [Image: Ricoh GR IV Monochrome I was so head over heels for the Ricoh GR IV Monochrome when I reviewed it that I recently bought one. A black-and-white-only fixed-lens camera is super niche, but for this photo nerd, it’s the perfect “artsy” pocket camera. I take it with me everywhere, even with my larger cameras during Verge events or wedding shoots. It’s a palate cleanser for everything from slice-of-life family snapshots to New York City street photography. I could achieve that with black-and-white film, but I inevitably fall off using my analog cameras. They say the best camera is the one you have with you, and the GR IV Monochrome is now always with me and always a delight. — Antonio G. Di Benedetto, laptop reviewer [Image: Keychron Nape Pro trackball The Nape Pro is the most unusual and best gadget I bought this year. It’s a bar-shaped device with six customizable buttons and a small trackball in the middle. I put it horizontally below my space bar, and once I tweaked the button layout, it became a daily driver. It feels like a cross between a trackpad and what I wish the TrackPoint on my ThinkPad was. The Nape Pro works over Bluetooth, USB-C, or 2.4GHz and supports up to 1000Hz polling. Battery life is fantastic, and it’s fully customizable. I still use a mouse at the big desk, but the Nape Pro is now as important to my portable setup as my laptop stand and keyboard. — Nathan Edwards, senior reviews editor [Image: Xteink X4 Pro Xteink redefined how small an e-reader can be, and while the company released several models in 2026 — including the X3, X4, and X4 Classic — the X4 Pro is the best of the bunch. It’s the company’s only model to include lighting and a touchscreen, which makes navigating Xteink’s software, or an excellent third-party alternative, much easier than using buttons alone. At $99, the X4 Pro is Xteink’s most expensive e-reader, and it doesn’t include access to an online bookstore, but with a 4.26-inch screen, you can slip it in a pocket alongside your phone. — Andrew Liszewski, senior reporter [Image: Steam Controller Months after reviewing it, I’m still a huge fan of Valve’s second-generation Steam Controller. It’s comfortable to hold for hours-long gaming sessions, has enough battery life that I never really think about it, and I love how I can customize nearly everything about the controller on a per-game basis inside Steam. If I have one knock against the controller, it’s that I don’t use the big touchpads all that often to replicate a mouse — but I have used them as giant buttons, which can be surprisingly useful in a pinch. I think I’ll be gaming with it for years to come.— Jay Peters, senior reporter [Image: Peak Design City Bags The Peak Design City Bags offer a unique way to hang them up wherever you are. They have a hook so you can hang them off a table and keep them off the dirty ground. The Verge’s Thomas Ricker, who reviewed the bags, said they made him a convert: “It beats setting a bag on the dirty ground or hanging it off the back of the chair where it will inevitably slide onto the floor, and it’s far better than holding a bag on your sweaty lap on a hot summer day.” He said they fit squarely in the everyday carry sweet spot for most people. — Jay Peters, senior reporter [Image: Asus Zephyrus I love ridiculous laptops, and there’s nothing quite as over-the-top as dual-screen models like Asus’ Zephyrus Duo and Zenbook Duo. The wildly expensive Zephyrus Duo gaming laptop is the perfect embodiment of this extravagant formula, with a mobile RTX 5090 GPU, dual 16-inch OLEDs, and a $5,500 price tag. It’s a marvel of maximalism. The more practical version is the latest Zenbook Duo — with its pair of 14-inch OLEDs and Intel Panther Lake chip — which is still pricey at $2,700, but no slouch for 1080p gaming on its integrated GPU. I wish these kinds of laptops had more accessible price points because they are an absolute treat to use. The more screens, the merrier. — Antonio G. Di Benedetto, laptop reviewer [Image: Nitecore NB10000 Gen 4 battery The Nitecore NB10000 Gen 4 power bank is the latest update in its line of ultralight battery packs. Nitecore has made a name for itself among endurance athletes and backpackers who want to pack as light as possible while still having enough power to recharge a phone and a smartwatch. The NB10000 has IPX7 protection to withstand rain or light immersion, two USB-C ports, a 10,000mAh silicon-carbon battery, and enough juice to top up an iPhone 15 Pro twice. It costs $84, which is a lot more than what you’d spend on a standard 10,000mAh battery, but it’s worth it for anyone who wants a thin and light battery that lasts. Oh, and did we mention there are RGB lights around the USB-C ports? — Todd Haselton, deputy reviews editor [Image: Aqara G400 Doorbell Camera Few products are truly perfect all-rounders in the smart home world, but Aqara’s G400 video doorbell comes close. It works with every platform, has local storage, and offers on-device AI to alert you to people at your door. It can record 24/7 because it’s hardwired, which also makes it a good choice for reliability, and there’s even the option of power over ethernet. It looks like a giant Mars bar on my front door, but I can forgive it for this because it does everything else very well. And at only $100, it is one of those rarities in tech today: a good product that’s affordable. — Jennifer Pattison Tuohy, senior reviewer [Image: Schlage Sense Pro The Schlage Sense Pro is the smartest lock on the block, thanks to ultra-wideband hands-free unlocking. With your phone in your pocket or bag, it can unlock as you approach, so you can just open the door — no need for keys or fiddling with an app. It’s like stepping into the future. While there are a couple of other UWB locks out there, the Schlage is my favorite because of its sleek, all-metal design, lack of a keyhole, and a very discreet keypad. Today, it works only with Apple Home Key for that magical unlocking, but thanks to its support for Aliro, the new smart lock standard, it should work with Android phones very soon. Jennifer Pattison Tuohy, senior reviewer
